\chapter{When It Happens, and What You Want}
\label{ch:ka-when-and-want}
\hlchaptermodality{72}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say when something happens, say what I want, and answer a choice with a preference.}

Complete KA-C72-prefer and answer an offered choice with what you like and what you do not.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bandāga]{\kn{ಬಂದಾಗ} (bandāga) — when somebody comes}

\label{lesson:KA-C72-when-clause}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which question word goes in front of a noun, and which one asks about a time?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬಂದಾಗ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬಂದಾಗ}} (\emph{bandāga}) — \textquotedblleft{}when (somebody) comes\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}on coming\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಯಾವಾಗ} asks about a time. This is how you answer with a whole event instead of a clock: \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಬಂದಾಗ}} (\emph{nīvu bandāga}) — \textquotedblleft{}when you come\textquotedblright{}.

It is \kn{ಬಾ} / \kn{ಬರು} (\textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}) in its past shape \kn{ಬಂದ}-, with \textbf{-\kn{ಆಗ}} (\emph{-āga}) on the end — and that ending is the same \kn{ಆಗ} that sits inside \kn{ಯಾವಾಗ}. \textquotedblleft{}When?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}when it happens\textquotedblright{} are built from one piece.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the when-clause comes first, and rides on the verb}]
Kannada's when-clause comes FIRST, and the main clause follows it. There is no word for \emph{when} standing between them; the ending on the verb is the join.

\textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಬಂದಾಗ} \kn{ಹೇಳಿ}} (\emph{nīvu bandāga hēḷi}) — \textquotedblleft{}tell me when you come.\textquotedblright{}

This is the same habit as the \kn{ಹೋಗಿ} of the everyday goodbye: Kannada hangs the first event on the verb's own ending and saves the finished verb for last. You have had that machinery since the farewell chapter; \kn{ಆಗ} is a second ending using the same slot, and the difference is only what it means — \kn{ಹೋಗಿ} says \emph{having done it}, \kn{ಬಂದಾಗ} says \emph{at the time of doing it}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two events in one sentence, and one of them says when.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bandāga}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nīvu bandāga hēḷi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yāvāga?} — then answer with an event instead of a time
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hōgi baruttēne}, and say which part is the participle
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ಅ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{innondu} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{cāpe}, \emph{nōḍu}, \emph{tinnu}, \emph{iru}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending makes a when-clause? (\textbf{-\kn{ಆಗ}}.) Does the clause come before or after the main one? (Before.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nanage cahā bēku]{\kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಬೇಕು} (nanage cahā bēku) — I want tea}

\label{lesson:KA-C72-want}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which ending makes a when-clause, and where does that clause sit?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಬೇಕು}}
\textbf{\kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಬೇಕು}} (\emph{nanage cahā bēku}) — \textquotedblleft{}I want tea.\textquotedblright{}

Literally: \textquotedblleft{}to me tea is wanted.\textquotedblright{} Wanting happens \textbf{to} you in Kannada, exactly as knowing does, so this is the dative sentence you already build with \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು}, with one word swapped.

This book gave you the refusal first. \kn{ಬೇಡ} (\emph{bēḍa}, \textquotedblleft{}no thank you\textquotedblright{}) has been your answer to an offer for a while, and it is the negative half of a pair whose positive half you did not have. The word doing the wanting here is that missing half.

On its own it answers an offer: somebody holds up the pot, you say the wanting word or you say \kn{ಬೇಡ}, and that is the whole exchange.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the pair, and the missing half}]
\kn{ಬೇಕು} and \kn{ಬೇಡ} are a matched pair, and neither of them names who is doing the wanting unless you put the dative in front. That is why a single word is a complete answer.

They are also inherited Dravidian rather than borrowed, and they answer Tamil \emph{vēṇṭum} and \emph{vēṇṭām} — which is worth noticing because the frame \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ} sits in was built for them first, and the Sanskrit word simply moved into the house.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Ask for something, and accept or refuse what is offered.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bēku}, then \emph{bēḍa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nanage cahā bēku}
  \item \emph{Say it:} somebody offers you something — accept it, then refuse it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bandāga}, then put it in a sentence
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{alla} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{innondu sala hēḷi} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{buṭṭi}, \emph{havāmāna}, \emph{caitra vaiśākha jyēṣṭha āṣāḍha śrāvaṇa bhādrapada āśvayuja kārtīka mārgaśira puṣya māgha phālguṇa}, \emph{vasanta ṛtu bēsige maḷegāla caḷigāla}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬೇಕು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}wanted\textquotedblright{}.) What is its negative twin? (\emph{bēḍa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ja]{\kn{ಜ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S150-letter-ja}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ವ} — what sound does it carry?

One character this time. It is in the words for a fever, a seed and a shoulder, and you have been reading past it for a long time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಜ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಜ}} — \emph{ja}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{j}, it is \textbf{ja}. Almost every Kannada word carrying it is a Sanskrit loan, which is a useful thing to notice: meeting \kn{ಜ} is a small clue about where a word came from.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಜ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಜ್ವರ}} \emph{jvara} — a fever
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಬೀಜ}} \emph{bīja} — a seed
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಭುಜ}} \emph{bhuja} — the shoulder
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಜ್ಜ}} \emph{ajja} — grandfather, and this one is native
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಜ}}
Put your pen on \kn{ಜ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಜ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಜ್ವರ}  ·  \kn{ಬೀಜ}  ·  \kn{ಅಜ್ಜ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಜ} three times, saying \emph{ja} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಜ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಜ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ja}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nimage kāphi iṣṭavā]{\kn{ನಿಮಗೆ} \kn{ಕಾಫಿ} \kn{ಇಷ್ಟವಾ} (nimage kāphi iṣṭavā) — do you like coffee?}

\label{lesson:KA-C72-do-you-like}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which character did you trace last, and how do you say you want something?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನಿಮಗೆ} \kn{ಕಾಫಿ} \kn{ಇಷ್ಟವಾ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನಿಮಗೆ} \kn{ಕಾಫಿ} \kn{ಇಷ್ಟವಾ}?} (\emph{nimage kāphi iṣṭavā?}) — \textquotedblleft{}do you like coffee?\textquotedblright{}

Everything in it is already yours. \kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಕನ್ನಡ} \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ} was the sentence with no verb in it — the liker in the dative, the thing liked plain, and nothing joining them. Turn it around and two things change:

\kn{ನನಗೆ} (\textquotedblleft{}to me\textquotedblright{}) becomes \kn{ನಿಮಗೆ} (\textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{}) — the same \textbf{-\kn{ಗೆ}} you have been putting on nouns, now on the polite \kn{ನೀವು}. And \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ} takes the question ending: \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ} + -\kn{ಆ}, with a \kn{ವ} slipped in to keep the two vowels apart, gives \kn{ಇಷ್ಟವಾ}.

That little \kn{ವ} is not a rule to learn. Kannada dislikes two vowels meeting and puts a \kn{ವ} or a \kn{ಯ} between them; you have heard it all along without noticing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A question about somebody else, instead of a statement about yourself. That is the turn a conversation needs.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nanage kāphi iṣṭa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nimage kāphi iṣṭavā?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask about something else you both know the word for
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bēku}, then \emph{bēḍa}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hālū illa, nīrū illa} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gottilla} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yāvāga} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ವ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{pātre}, \emph{cāku}, \emph{tale kai}, \emph{kappu biḷi kempu nīli}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word changed to move the sentence from you to them? (\emph{nanage} to \emph{nimage}.) Which ending made it a question? (\textbf{-\kn{ಆ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nanage cahā iṣṭa, kāphi alla]{\kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ}, \kn{ಕಾಫಿ} \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ} (nanage cahā iṣṭa, kāphi alla) — I prefer tea, not coffee}

\label{lesson:KA-C72-prefer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: ask somebody whether they like coffee.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ}, \kn{ಕಾಫಿ} \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ}, \kn{ಕಾಫಿ} \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{nanage cahā iṣṭa, kāphi alla}) — \textquotedblleft{}I like tea, not coffee.\textquotedblright{}

Somebody offers you the choice with \kn{ಅಥವಾ}; this is the answer. Kannada has no single word for \emph{prefer}. What it does is say what you like and then deny the alternative — the liking sentence you already own, with \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ} on the end of the one you are turning down.

That is a real economy rather than a gap: \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ} denies a description, and \textquotedblleft{}coffee\textquotedblright{} is exactly a description here of what you like. The two halves of the sentence are doing the two things this chapter and the last one taught.

\textbf{\kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಅಥವಾ} \kn{ಕಾಫಿ}? — \kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ}, \kn{ಕಾಫಿ} \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}.} Question and answer, both of them built out of pieces you were given one at a time.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A choice offered, a choice answered. That exchange needs a word for \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}, a word for \textquotedblleft{}like\textquotedblright{} and a word for \textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{}, and all three are now yours.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cahā athavā kāphi?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nanage cahā iṣṭa, kāphi alla}
  \item \emph{Say it:} swap them round and answer the other way
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yāva}, then ask which of two things somebody wants
  \item \emph{Recall:} the whole chapter — \emph{bandāga}, \emph{nanage cahā bēku}, \emph{\kn{ಜ}}, \emph{nimage kāphi iṣṭavā}, and this one
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nanagū gottilla} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yāva} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{peṭṭige}, \emph{sōmavāra maṅgaḷavāra budhavāra guruvāra śukravāra śanivāra bhānuvāra}, \emph{ombattu}, \emph{ēḷu}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Kannada say you prefer one thing to another? (Say what you like, then deny the other with \emph{alla}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
